steps.label: Facts
steps.body:
Causal chain:
Electrified instruments → each musician plays louder → fewer musicians per band, on average

Pivot (nevertheless):
Electrified instruments → more musicians playing popular music professionally

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
On a Most Supported question, cause and effect is the first thing to read for, and this paragraph is full of it: electrification enabled more volume, the extra volume shrank the average band, and electrification also raised the number of professional musicians.

Then the pivot word "Nevertheless" sets two results of electrification against each other:
1. Fewer musicians per band, on average.
2. More professional musicians overall.

When a pivot creates a math tension like this, the correct answer usually resolves it. So ask: if each band has fewer people, how can there be more people in total?

There have to be more bands. Run numbers. Say there used to be 80 bands of 10, which is 800 musicians. If bands now average 5 and we have 1,000 musicians, we need 200 bands. Smaller bands plus more musicians forces the number of bands up.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer that says the number of bands has gone up. A safe answer could also simply restate the chain from electrification to smaller bands, but the math inference about more bands is the one the paragraph is built to test.

notes.body: The paragraph only counts musicians who play popular music professionally. Amateurs never come up, so we have no information about whether their numbers rose, fell, or stayed the same.

The paragraph says instruments were electrified. It never says whether any musician can play a nonelectric instrument, let alone most of them. A claim about musicians' skills has nothing to stand on here.

This is the most popular wrong answer. The *average* band got smaller. Some bands could have grown, but nothing in the passage says so, and the average would also fall if every single band shrank. An answer that is merely possible isn't supported.

Fewer musicians per band, more musicians overall. The only way both are true is more bands. Picture 100 musicians in bands of 5: 20 bands. Now 150 musicians in bands of 3: 50 bands. Electrification drives both trends, so crediting it with the extra bands is fair.

This is one way to spread musicians across more bands, but nothing in the paragraph says anyone plays in more than one band. The math only forces more bands; it does not tell us how musicians are spread across them. Every musician could play in exactly one band and the facts still hold.

old_steps.label: Facts
old_steps.body:
causal (by, which has enabled, because, increased)
electrical >> play w/ >> avg # of musicians instruments more volume per band decreased
pivot (nevertheless)
electrical >> greater # of professional instruments musicians

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body:
The #1 thing we read for on Most Supported is Cause / Effect relationships, and we got four of them here.
There's a causal chain, and then a pivot that creates a **mathy tension** between two different things caused by electrification: 1. fewer musicians per band 2. more musicians overall When we see a Pivot creating a mathy tension, the correct answer usually addresses / resolves that tension.
If we have fewer musicians in each band nowadays, how can also have more musicians total?
We would need there to be more bands than before.
Maybe there used to be 10 ppl / band, and there were 80 bands, giving us 800 musicians.
If we only have 5 ppl / band now and want to end up with 1000 musicians (some larger number), then we'd need 200 bands.

old_steps.label: Goal
old_steps.body: The correct answer will probably reward us for understanding the causal chain between electrified instruments and fewer people per band, or it'll test this mathy inference that there are more bands.

old_notes.body: The passage is about professional musicians. Amateurs never come up.
Nothing tells us which instruments musicians can play.

This is the most popular wrong answer. The *average* band got smaller. Some bands could have grown, but nothing in the passage says so, and the average would also fall if every single band shrank. An answer that is merely possible isn't supported.

Fewer musicians per band, more musicians overall. The only way both are true is more bands. Picture 100 musicians in bands of 5: 20 bands. Now 150 musicians in bands of 3: 50 bands. Electrification drives both trends, so crediting it with the extra bands is fair.
Nothing tells us whether musicians play in more than one band.

steps.label: Premises
steps.body:
In a six-month study, an afternoon-exercise group got 33% more deep sleep than a control group.
Afternoon exercise tends to raise body temperature slightly until after bedtime, and this extra heat induces deeper sleep.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The study gives us a result: afternoon exercisers got 33 percent more deep sleep than the control group. Then the researcher explains why: afternoon exercise raises body temperature slightly until after bedtime, and "this extra heat induces deeper sleep."

That last clause is the key. The researcher does not say exercise itself deepens sleep. The researcher says the extra heat does. So the cause is the heat, and exercise is just one way to produce it. Anything else that leaves you slightly warmer at bedtime should have the same effect.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer that applies the heat mechanism to some other source of warmth near bedtime, worded modestly ("likely", "tends to"). Expect the wrong answers to overreach with words like "required", "the best way", or "no one".

notes.body: "Required" means no one gets adequate deep sleep without afternoon exercise. The study only shows that exercisers got more deep sleep than a group that exercised little or not at all. And the mechanism points the other way: if heat is the cause, other sources of heat could do the job without exercise.

The mechanism depends on body heat lasting until after bedtime. Morning exercise never comes up, and its heat could easily wear off long before night. Nothing lets us compare morning exercise with afternoon exercise.
"The best way" needs a comparison with every other way to get deep sleep. The researcher describes one thing that helps. That supports "this works," not "nothing works better."

This is the most popular wrong answer. "No one" covers every person in the control group. They exercised little, but someone could have been warmed by a hot meal or a fever. The study reports group results, not every individual.

The researcher says deeper sleep comes from "this extra heat," a slight rise in body temperature that lasts past bedtime. A warm bath just before bed produces that same condition, so the mechanism predicts it should help too. Notice the move: when a stimulus names the mechanism behind a result, the supported answer often applies that mechanism to a new case. "Will likely" is as strong as the mechanism allows, and no stronger.

old_steps.label: Premises
old_steps.body:
In a six-month study, an afternoon-exercise group got 33% more deep sleep than a control group.
Afternoon exercise tends to raise body temperature slightly until after bedtime, and this extra heat induces deeper sleep.

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body: The researcher is offering a mechanism: a slight rise in body temperature lasting until after bedtime causes deeper sleep. Anything that produces that same condition (slight body-temperature rise persisting until bedtime) should produce deeper sleep too — even if it is not exercise.

old_steps.label: Goal
old_steps.body: Find an answer that the mechanism statement directly supports. Be wary of answers that overstate (e.g., "necessary," "best way," "no one"). The right answer should be a modest extension of the mechanism, not a sweeping claim.

old_notes.body: "Required" means no one gets enough deep sleep without afternoon exercise. The study only shows exercisers got *more* deep sleep.
The mechanism depends on body heat lasting until bedtime. Morning exercise is never discussed, and its heat could easily wear off by night.
"The best way" needs a comparison with every other method. The passage describes one method that works.

This is the most popular wrong answer. "No one" covers every person in the control group. They exercised little, but someone could have been warmed by a hot meal or a fever. The study reports group results, not every individual.

The researcher says the deep sleep comes from a slight rise in body temperature lasting past bedtime. A warm bath right before bed creates that same condition, so it should help too. "Will likely" is exactly as strong as the mechanism allows.

steps.label: Statements
steps.body:
The Sapir-Whorf hypothesis: a society's world view is influenced by the language its members speak.

Pivot (but): the hypothesis lacks the verifiability of hypotheses in physical science.

Reason (since): it is not clear that the hypothesis could be tested.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
No conditional or causal chain here. The useful part is the pivot and its reason. The linguist is not attacking the hypothesis as false. The complaint is about verifiability: it is not clear the hypothesis could be tested at all.

What follows from a hypothesis that may not be testable? We cannot confirm it, and we cannot refute it. So we are in no position to say whether it is true. Notice what does not follow: that it is false, or that it should be ignored. The linguist says nothing about either.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for a modest answer saying we cannot currently tell whether the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis is true. Expect wrong answers to call it false, or to jump to rules about which hypotheses deserve attention, or to say "only" physical science can be verified.

notes.body: Lacking a test is not evidence against a claim. The linguist says we may not be able to check the hypothesis, which leaves it unconfirmed, not probably false. If we cannot test something, we have no grounds to call it likely true or likely false.

The linguist compares this one hypothesis with physical science. That tells us physical-science hypotheses are verifiable, not that they are the only verifiable ones. Plenty of hypotheses outside physical science could be testable; the passage just never discusses them.

This turns a fact about the hypothesis into a rule about what we should take seriously. The linguist never says what deserves serious consideration, so nothing here supports dismissing unverifiable hypotheses.

If it is not clear the hypothesis could even be tested, then it has not been confirmed, and we have no reliable way to tell whether it is true. That leaves us exactly where D says: we do not know. Notice how little D claims. It takes the linguist's point about testing one small step, which is what a supported answer usually does.

Two problems. Like C, it adds a rule about what deserves to be taken seriously, which the linguist never states. And like B, it says "only" physical science, when the passage compares one hypothesis with physical science and says nothing about any other field.

old_steps.label: Given
old_steps.body:
The Sapir-Whorf hypothesis states that a society's world view is influenced by the language or languages its members speak.
But this hypothesis does not have the verifiability of hypotheses of physical science.
It is not clear that the hypothesis could be tested.

old_notes.body: The hypothesis has not been verified, but to say that it is probably false goes too far.
While the hypotheses of physical science are verifiable, they need not be the only verifiable hypotheses.
Which hypotheses ought to be seriously considered is not discussed in the statements.
This is supported by the second statement.
Which hypotheses ought to be taken seriously is not discussed in the statements.

steps.label: Statements
steps.body:
1. Articles criticizing the environmental movement now appear regularly in newspapers.

2. Winslow's explanation: this is due less to antienvironmental bias in the media than to editors preferring articles that seem "daring," because they seem to challenge prevailing political positions.

3. The commentator agrees: "It is true that editors like to run antienvironmental pieces mainly because they seem to challenge the political orthodoxy."

4. Pivot (but): serious environmentalism is not politically orthodox, so antienvironmentalists are not really dissidents, even if they have succeeded in selling themselves as renegades.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
This is a concede-then-pivot paragraph, and the hard part is sorting what the commentator accepts from what the commentator rejects.

Winslow makes a claim about editors: they publish antienvironmental articles because those articles seem daring, seeming to challenge prevailing positions. The commentator says "It is true" and repeats that point almost word for word. So the commentator accepts Winslow's account of what editors prefer.

Then comes "But." The pivot does not deny the editors' preference. It denies that the articles actually are daring. Environmentalism is not the orthodox position, so attacking it is not a real challenge to orthodoxy, and the critics are not real dissidents. In short: the articles only seem daring, and that appearance is what editors are buying.

On a hard Most Supported question, the conceded part is often where the right answer hides, because the pivot pulls attention away from it.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer saying Winslow is right about the editors: they prefer articles that seem to challenge prevailing positions. Expect traps that treat the "But" as a rejection of Winslow's whole explanation, that say environmentalism is the orthodox view, or that deny the critics' success at looking like renegades.

notes.body: The commentator says outright, "It is true that editors like to run antienvironmental pieces mainly because they seem to challenge the political orthodoxy." That is Winslow's claim about editors, confirmed. The "But" that follows attacks the articles, not Winslow's account of editors. The move to repeat: when a speaker concedes part of someone's view and then pivots, sort which part was conceded. The conceded part is safe ground for a Most Supported answer.

The commentator concedes the opposite: antienvironmentalists "can hardly claim to be dissidents, however much they may have succeeded in selling themselves as renegades." That phrasing grants, or at least allows, that the self-promotion worked. The commentator's complaint is that the image is false, not that it failed to sell.

This is the most tempting trap, because the commentator does push back on something. But the commentator agrees that editors run these pieces mainly because they seem to challenge orthodoxy, and that preference fits articles appearing regularly. So Winslow's explanation does account for the frequency. What the commentator rejects is the idea that the pieces really are daring, which is a different claim from why editors publish them.

The commentator says the reverse: "serious environmentalism is by no means politically orthodox." Environmentalism is the position the critics attack, so the attacked position is not the prevailing one. That is exactly why the critics are not real dissidents.

The commentator describes the present: what editors prefer and where environmentalism stands now. Nothing is said about where environmentalism is headed, so a prediction that it will "eventually become" the prevailing position has no support.

old_steps.label: Given
old_steps.body: Recently, articles criticizing the environmental movement have been appearing regularly in newspapers. According to Winslow, this is due not so much to an antienvironmental bias among the media as to a preference on the part of newspaper editors for articles that seem “daring” in that they seem to challenge prevailing political positions. It is true that editors like to run antienvironmental pieces mainly because they seem to challenge the political orthodoxy. But serious environmentalism is by no means politically orthodox, and antienvironmentalists can hardly claim to be dissidents, however much they may have succeeded in selling themselves as renegades.

old_notes.body: This is supported by the second and third statements.
The fourth statement undermines this answer.

This is undermined by the first, second, and third statements. Winslow’s explanation is consonant with the frequency since Winslow is correct about the editors’ preference for articles that seem daring and antienvironmental articles have been appearing regularly.
The fourth statement undermines this answer.
The statements do not make any predictions.

steps.label: Statements
steps.body:
1. Boat engine noise runs from 100 to 3,000 hertz, a range that overlaps the range killer whales use to communicate.

2. Pivot (though): the whales do not seem to behave differently around running engines, but engine noise can be loud enough to damage their hearing over time.

3. Therefore, _______ .

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
On a logical completion, the blank is the conclusion, so we ask what the premises are building toward.

Look for the overlap. Premise one connects engine noise to communication: the noise sits in the whales' communication range. Premise two connects engine noise to hearing damage. Put them together: boat noise can damage the very hearing the whales use to communicate.

The "Though" clause matters too. The whales do not act differently around engines, which might make us think the noise is harmless. The author is warning against that: no visible reaction does not mean no harm.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for a conclusion like "boat engine noise may harm the whales' ability to communicate, even though they show no reaction." Keep it soft, since the premises only say the damage "can" happen, and keep it tied to communication.

notes.body: Nothing in the statements compares younger and older whales. The passage says engine noise "can be loud enough to damage their hearing over time," but it never says how well whales of any age tolerate the noise, so this conclusion has no support.

The only thing we hear about whale behavior around engines is that they "do not seem to behave differently." If anything, that cuts against B, since attempting less communication would be a change in behavior. The premises are about harm to hearing, not about choosing to stay quiet.

Both premises meet here. The noise overlaps the frequencies the whales communicate in, and it can damage their hearing. A whale that hears worse in the very range it uses to talk can have trouble communicating. Notice the soft wording: "may impair." The premises say damage "can" happen, so a conclusion that claims only possibility is exactly as strong as the evidence. On a completion question, look for the answer that joins every premise and claims no more than they allow.
The passage never says where whales prefer to be. And it reports that whales do not seem to behave differently around engines, which gives us no sign that they seek out or avoid boat traffic at all.

Food never comes up. To get here we would need to know the whales use hearing to hunt, and the passage only ties their hearing to communication. "Would probably be more successful" also claims an effect the premises never measure.

old_steps.label: Given
old_steps.body: Engine noise from boats traveling through killer whales’ habitats ranges in frequency from 100 hertz to 3,000 hertz, an acoustical range that overlaps that in which the whales communicate through screams and squeals. Though killer whales do not seem to behave differently around running boat engines, engine noise from boats can be loud enough to damage their hearing over time.

old_notes.body: Nothing in the statements compares younger and older whales. The passage says engine noise "can be loud enough to damage their hearing over time," but it never says how well whales of any age tolerate the noise, so this conclusion has no support.
When killer whales attempt to communicate is not discussed in the statements.
Since engine noise from boats can damage killer whales’ hearing, it may impair their ability to communicate.
The areas preferred by killer whales is not discussed in the statements.
How successful whales would be in finding food is not discussed in the statements.

steps.label: Statements
steps.body:
All of this is about early times, before irrigation became feasible away from water.

Early urban societies could not have been maintained without large-scale farming nearby.
Early urban society → large-scale farming nearby

This is because other methods of food acquisition, such as foraging, cannot support populations as dense as urban ones.

Large-scale farming requires irrigation, which remained unfeasible in areas far from rivers or lakes until more recent times.
Large-scale farming → irrigation
Early times and far from rivers or lakes → no irrigation

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Three conditionals, and they share terms: large-scale farming appears in the first and second rules, irrigation in the second and third. Shared terms are a signal to chain.

Early urban society → large-scale farming → irrigation

Now look at the irrigation fact. Far from rivers or lakes, early irrigation was not feasible. Run the chain backward with contrapositives: no irrigation means no large-scale farming, and no large-scale farming means no early urban society.

Keep the time limit in view. Irrigation became feasible far from water "in more recent times," so the conclusion only holds for early times.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer saying that, in early times, urban societies could not be maintained far from rivers or lakes. Watch for answers that drop "early," drop "urban," or claim anything about where people actually lived.

notes.body: The passage tells us where early urban societies could be maintained, not where most people lived. If most early peoples lived in small rural groups that foraged, they could have lived anywhere. A claim about the whole population needs facts about the whole population.

Two problems. First, B is about all societies, but the passage says only that urban ones need large-scale farming; a small foraging society far from water breaks no rule in the passage. Second, B has no time limit, while the passage says irrigation became feasible far from water in more recent times. A modern society far from rivers could farm with irrigation, so B's "only if" requirement does not follow.

This follows from combining the three conditional statements, read in early times.

Far from rivers or lakes → no irrigation
No irrigation → no large-scale farming
No large-scale farming → no urban society
So: far from rivers or lakes → no urban society

The second and third lines are contrapositives of the rules in the stimulus. When a Most Supported paragraph hands you several conditionals that share terms, link them and look for the answer that joins the two ends.

The passage points the other way. Early urban societies required large-scale farming, and large-scale farming requires irrigation.

Early urban society → large-scale farming → irrigation

Being near a river or lake makes irrigation possible; it does not remove the need for it. So D is contradicted, not supported.
Rural societies never come up. The passage says foraging cannot feed dense urban populations, but it says nothing about how much rural societies foraged compared with how much they farmed.

old_steps.label: Given
old_steps.body:
Early urban societies could not have been maintained without large-scale farming nearby.
US → LSF

This is because other methods of food acquisition, such as foraging, cannot support populations as dense as urban ones.

Large-scale farming requires irrigation, which remained unfeasible in areas far from rivers or lakes until more recent times.
LSF → IR
~RL → ~IR

old_notes.body: Where people actually lived in early times is not discussed in the statements.
This goes too far by changing the subject from urban societies to societies more generally.

This follows from combining the three conditional statements.

~RL → ~IR
~IR → ~LSF
~LSF → ~US
∴ ~RL → ~US

Urban societies require large-scale farming, and large-scale farming requires irrigation.

US → LSF → IR

So urban societies with farms near rivers or lakes still rely on irrigation, which contradicts D.
Early rural societies are not discussed in the statements.

steps.label: Statements
steps.body:
Any good garden compost may appropriately be used for soil drainage and fertility.
Good compost → appropriate for drainage and fertility

The best compost is 40 to 60 percent organic matter and is dark brown in color.
Best compost → 40 to 60 percent organic and dark brown

However, compost that emits a strong ammonia smell should not be used for drainage and fertility, for that smell means that the organic matter has not sufficiently decomposed.
Strong ammonia smell → not appropriate for drainage and fertility
Strong ammonia smell → not sufficiently decomposed

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Two rules talk about the same thing: whether compost may be used for drainage and fertility.

Good compost → appropriate for drainage and fertility
Strong ammonia smell → not appropriate for drainage and fertility

Take the contrapositive of the first rule: not appropriate → not good compost. Now chain:

Strong ammonia smell → not appropriate → not good compost

So any compost with a strong ammonia smell is not good compost, no matter what else is true of it.

The best-compost sentence is a distraction. It gives requirements for the best compost, so it can only tell us when something is not the best. It can never prove a compost is good or best.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer saying that compost with a strong ammonia smell is not good compost. Expect wrong answers that use the 40 to 60 percent or dark brown features to prove a compost is good, or that invent a link between organic percentage and decomposition.

notes.body: The passage links decomposition to ammonia smell, not to the percentage of organic matter. 80 percent tells us this is not the best compost, since the best is 40 to 60 percent, but nothing says high organic content means poor decomposition.

The passage never says any compost harms soil. Compost under 40 percent organic matter and not dark brown fails the description of the best compost, so it is not the best. Not the best is a long way from "will make soil less fertile and will worsen soil drainage." It could still be good compost, or merely unhelpful.

This tries to prove a compost is good, and nothing in the passage gives us a way to prove that. The 40 to 60 percent figure is a requirement for the best compost, not a guarantee: best → 40 to 60 percent does not give us 40 to 60 percent → good. And sufficient decomposition only removes one reason to reject a compost. Clearing one obstacle does not make it good.

We only know that a strong ammonia smell means the organic matter is not sufficiently decomposed. "Sufficiently" is far short of "completely." The passage never describes the decomposition level of the best compost at all.

Chain the first and third statements. Strong ammonia smell → not appropriate for drainage and fertility. Contrapositive of the first rule: not appropriate → not good compost. So smelly compost is not good compost, whatever its color. The dark brown detail is bait: it is a feature of the best compost, but meeting a requirement never proves the label, and the ammonia smell rules the compost out anyway.

old_steps.label: Given
old_steps.body:
Any good garden compost may appropriately be used for soil drainage and fertility.
GGC → SDF

The best compost is 40 to 60 percent organic matter and is dark brown in color.
BC → 40-60% + DB

However, compost that emits a strong ammonia smell should not be used for drainage and fertility, for that smell means that the organic matter has not sufficiently decomposed.
SA → ~SDF
SA → ~D

old_notes.body: The statements do not indicate that there is a relationship between the percent of organic material and the level of decomposition.
While compost that is less than 40 percent organic matter is not the best compost, that does not imply that it will make soil less fertile and will worsen soil drainage.

This reverses the first statement.

SDF → GGC

Being sufficiently decomposed only removes one reason not to use compost. Nothing in the stimulus says that compost meeting these conditions is good.
The statements do not indicate that organic matter is completely decomposed.

This follows from the first and third statements.

SA → ~SDF
~SDF → ~GGC
∴ SA → ~GGC

Compost with a strong ammonia smell shouldn't be used for drainage and fertility, and any good compost can be. So smelly compost isn't good compost, whatever its color.
